topics.title: File Systems versus Database Systems
topics.definition: A file system stores data in separate application files, while a DBMS stores it centrally with controlled sharing and integrity.

children.title: Drawbacks of file processing
children.definition: Data redundancy, inconsistency, difficulty of concurrent access, weak security and program data dependence.

children.title: Advantages of a DBMS
children.definition: Controlled redundancy, shared data, integrity constraints, backup and recovery, security and data independence.

children.title: When a DBMS is not suitable
children.definition: Small single user applications with simple fixed data may not justify the cost and complexity of a DBMS.

topics.title: Data Models
topics.definition: A data model is a collection of concepts for describing the structure of a database and the operations allowed on it.

children.title: Hierarchical model
children.definition: Organises data as a tree of parent and child records, where each child has exactly one parent.

children.title: Network model
children.definition: Uses a graph of records where a child may have more than one parent, handled through sets and pointers.

children.title: Relational model
children.definition: Represents data as tables of rows and columns with keys and relationships expressed by matching values.

children.title: Object based and object relational models
children.definition: Store complex objects, classes and inheritance, with object relational systems adding these ideas to relational tables.

children.title: Entity relationship model
children.definition: A conceptual, diagrammatic model of entities, attributes and relationships used before implementation.

topics.title: DBMS Architecture
topics.definition: A DBMS is organised in levels so that users, the logical design and the physical storage remain independent of one another.

children.title: Three schema architecture
children.definition: External or view level for individual users, conceptual level for the logical design and internal level for physical storage.

children.title: Data abstraction
children.definition: Hides storage detail from users and shows only the level of detail each user needs.

children.title: Database administrator and users
children.definition: The DBA designs and maintains the schema and controls access, while end users, application programmers and analysts use the data.

children.title: Database languages
children.definition: DDL defines structures, DML manipulates data, DCL controls privileges and TCL manages transactions.

topics.title: Data Independence
topics.definition: Data independence means that a change at one level of the schema does not force changes at a higher level.

children.title: Logical data independence
children.definition: Changing the conceptual schema, such as adding a column, need not change the external views or the application programs.

children.title: Physical data independence
children.definition: Changing storage structures such as adding an index need not change the conceptual schema.

children.title: How independence is achieved
children.definition: By keeping separate schema levels and mapping each level to the next.

topics.title: Data Modelling Using the Entity Relationship Model
topics.definition: The ER model describes data as entities, their attributes and the relationships between them, drawn as a diagram.

children.title: Entity and entity set
children.definition: An entity is a real world object such as a student and an entity set is a collection of similar entities.

children.title: Attributes and their types
children.definition: Simple, composite, single valued, multivalued, derived and key attributes describe the properties of an entity.

children.title: Relationship and relationship set
children.definition: An association among entities such as enrols between student and course.

children.title: Degree and cardinality ratio
children.definition: Degree counts participating entity sets; cardinality is one to one, one to many, many to one or many to many.

children.title: Participation constraints
children.definition: Total participation means every entity takes part, partial means only some do.

children.title: Keys in ER design
children.definition: Super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key identify entities and link them.

children.title: Weak entity set
children.definition: An entity set without a key of its own, identified only through its owner entity with a partial key.

children.title: ER diagram notation
children.definition: Rectangles for entities, ellipses for attributes, diamonds for relationships, double lines for total participation.

topics.title: Enhanced ER Modelling
topics.definition: Enhanced ER modelling adds abstraction tools such as specialisation, generalisation, aggregation and categories.

children.title: Specialisation and generalisation
children.definition: Specialisation splits a superclass into subclasses, generalisation combines similar entities into a superclass.

children.title: Attribute inheritance
children.definition: A subclass inherits all attributes of its superclass and adds its own.

children.title: Constraints on specialisation
children.definition: Disjoint or overlapping subclasses, and total or partial participation in the specialisation.

children.title: Aggregation
children.definition: Treats a relationship as a higher level entity so it can take part in another relationship.

children.title: Category and union type
children.definition: A subclass whose members come from a union of several different superclasses, shown with a union circle.

modules.title: Relational Model, SQL, Design and Normalisation

topics.title: Relational Model Concepts
topics.definition: The relational model stores data in relations (tables) of tuples (rows) and attributes (columns) drawn from domains.

children.title: Relation, tuple, attribute and domain
children.definition: A relation is a table, a tuple is a row, an attribute is a named column and a domain is the set of allowed values.

children.title: Degree and cardinality
children.definition: Degree counts the attributes or columns and cardinality counts the tuples or rows.

children.title: Keys of a relation
children.definition: Super key uniquely identifies a tuple, candidate keys are minimal super keys, one becomes the primary key and foreign keys reference other relations.

children.title: Integrity constraints
children.definition: Entity integrity forbids NULL primary keys and referential integrity requires a foreign key to match some existing primary key or be NULL.

children.title: Codd rules
children.definition: Twelve rules described by E F Codd that a full relational DBMS should satisfy.

topics.title: Relational Algebra
topics.definition: Relational algebra is a procedural query language of operators that take relations and produce a new relation.

children.title: Selection and projection
children.definition: Selection (sigma) chooses rows satisfying a condition; projection (pi) chooses a subset of columns.

children.title: Set operations
children.definition: Union, intersection, set difference and Cartesian product combine relations with compatible schemas.

children.title: Join operations
children.definition: Theta join, equi join and natural join combine matching rows; outer joins keep unmatched rows padded with NULL.

children.title: Division operation
children.definition: Returns tuples of one relation that match every tuple of another, used for questions like "students who took all courses".

children.title: Renaming and assignment
children.definition: The rho operator renames relations or attributes and the assignment operator names intermediate results.

topics.title: SQL: Basic and Complex Queries
topics.definition: SQL is the standard language for defining and querying relational databases, written as declarative statements.

children.title: DDL, DML, DCL and TCL
children.definition: DDL creates and alters structures, DML selects and modifies rows, DCL grants privileges and TCL commits or rolls back transactions.

children.title: Basic SELECT queries
children.definition: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition with DISTINCT, ORDER BY, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE.

children.title: Aggregate functions and grouping
children.definition: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX with GROUP BY and HAVING for conditions on groups.

children.title: Joins in SQL
children.definition: Inner join, left, right and full outer joins in both the classic and ANSI syntax.

children.title: Subqueries and correlated queries
children.definition: Nested SELECT statements, including EXISTS, ANY and ALL comparisons against inner results.

children.title: UPDATE, DELETE and INSERT
children.definition: Statements that modify the contents of existing relations.

children.title: Views
children.definition: A stored query acting as a virtual table, used for security and simplified access; updatable only under restrictions.

children.title: Constraints
children.definition: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK and DEFAULT enforce rules at the schema level.

topics.title: Relational Calculus
topics.definition: Relational calculus is a non procedural query language that describes what result is wanted rather than how to compute it.

children.title: Tuple relational calculus
children.definition: Describes the set of tuples t for which a predicate is true, written as {t | P(t)}.

children.title: Domain relational calculus
children.definition: Describes the result by listing the domains of its attributes with conditions on them.

children.title: Expressiveness and safety
children.definition: Both calculi are equivalent in power to relational algebra; safe expressions avoid infinite results.

topics.title: Overview of Commercial RDBMSs
topics.definition: Commercial systems such as Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and DB2 implement SQL with vendor extensions.

children.title: Features to compare
children.definition: Storage limits, concurrency control, recovery, partitioning, security, replication and cost.

children.title: Oracle and SQL Server
children.definition: Enterprise systems with PL/SQL and T-SQL procedural extensions and rich administration tools.

children.title: MySQL and PostgreSQL
children.definition: Widely used open source systems, one favoured for web applications and the other for standards compliance.

topics.title: Database Design and Functional Dependencies
topics.definition: Good relational design starts from dependencies among attributes that reveal redundancy and update anomalies.

children.title: Informal design guidelines
children.definition: Keep semantics clear, reduce redundancy and avoid NULL heavy relations.

children.title: Functional dependency
children.definition: X determines Y means any two tuples agreeing on X must also agree on Y, written X -> Y.

children.title: Partial and transitive dependency
children.definition: A partial dependency uses only part of a composite key; a transitive dependency reaches a non-key attribute through another non-key attribute.

children.title: Armstrong axioms
children.definition: Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity generate all dependencies, with union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity as derived rules.

children.title: Closure and candidate key computation
children.definition: The closure of an attribute set gives everything it determines, and a minimal attribute set whose closure is the whole relation is a candidate key.

children.title: Canonical cover
children.definition: A minimal equivalent set of functional dependencies with no redundant dependencies or attributes.

children.title: Decomposition and its properties
children.definition: Splitting a relation into smaller relations, checked for lossless join and dependency preservation.

topics.title: Normal Forms
topics.definition: Normalisation removes redundancy and anomalies by checking a relation against progressively stricter normal forms.

children.title: Why normalisation is needed
children.definition: Unnormalised relations suffer update, insertion and deletion anomalies along with wasted space.

children.title: 1NF (First Normal Form)
children.definition: All attributes hold atomic single values - no multivalued attributes or repeating groups.

children.title: 2NF (Second Normal Form)
children.definition: In 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on part of a candidate key.

children.title: 3NF (Third Normal Form)
children.definition: In 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.

children.title: BCNF (Boyce Codd Normal Form)
children.definition: For every non trivial dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key - stricter than 3NF.

children.title: 4NF (Fourth Normal Form)
children.definition: In BCNF and free of multivalued dependencies, which occur when independent multivalued facts are stored together.

children.title: 5NF (Fifth Normal Form)
children.definition: Also called project join normal form, where a relation cannot be decomposed any further without loss.

children.title: Denormalisation
children.definition: Deliberately relaxing normal forms to reduce joins and improve read performance in reporting systems.

topics.title: Query Processing and Cost Estimation
topics.definition: Query processing turns an SQL statement into an executable plan whose cost is estimated to pick the cheapest strategy.

children.title: Parsing, validation and translation
children.definition: The query is checked for syntax and semantics and converted into a relational algebra expression.

children.title: Optimisation and plan generation
children.definition: Equivalent expressions and access paths are compared to choose an efficient execution plan.

children.title: Algorithms for executing query operations
children.definition: Full table scan or index scan for selection, nested loop, sort merge and hash join for joins, external sorting for large data.

children.title: Cost estimation
children.definition: Estimates block transfers and disk seeks using statistics such as number of tuples, block factor and selectivity.

children.title: Heuristic optimisation rules
children.definition: Push selections down, then projections, and perform the most restrictive operations first.

topics.title: Transaction Processing and Properties
topics.definition: A transaction is a logical unit of work that must either complete fully or leave the database unchanged.

children.title: Transaction operations
children.definition: read_item, write_item, commit and rollback are the basic operations of a transaction.

children.title: ACID properties
children.definition: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability describe the guarantees a DBMS must provide.

children.title: Transaction states
children.definition: Active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted states trace the life of a transaction.

children.title: Desirable additional properties
children.definition: Fine granularity of data items and protection from crashes and concurrent interference.

topics.title: Serializability
topics.definition: A schedule is serializable when its effect equals that of some serial order of the same transactions.

children.title: Schedules and their types
children.definition: Serial schedules run transactions one after another; non-serial schedules interleave them.

children.title: Conflict serializability
children.definition: Two different transactions accessing the same item with at least one write conflict; the precedence graph must be acyclic.

children.title: View serializability
children.definition: A weaker condition requiring the same reads-from relations and the same final writes.

children.title: Recoverable and cascade-less schedules
children.definition: A schedule is recoverable if a transaction commits only after all transactions it read from have committed; cascading rollback is avoided by strict schedules.

topics.title: Transaction Support in SQL
topics.definition: SQL supports explicit transaction control with COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT statements and isolation levels.

children.title: COMMIT and ROLLBACK
children.definition: COMMIT makes changes permanent while ROLLBACK undoes changes of the current transaction.

children.title: SAVEPOINT and partial rollback
children.definition: Marks an intermediate point to which the transaction can roll back without losing earlier work.

children.title: Isolation levels
children.definition: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE trade correctness against concurrency.

children.title: Concurrency problems controlled by levels
children.definition: Dirty read, non repeatable read and phantom read.

topics.title: Locking Techniques
topics.definition: Locking prevents conflicting accesses by making a transaction acquire a lock before reading or writing an item.

children.title: Shared and exclusive locks
children.definition: A shared lock allows reading by many transactions while an exclusive lock allows one writer and blocks everyone else.

children.title: Binary locking versus shared exclusive locking
children.definition: Binary locks are locked or unlocked; shared exclusive locks distinguish readers from writers.

children.title: Two phase locking (2PL)
children.definition: A growing phase acquires locks and a shrinking phase releases them, which guarantees conflict serializability.

children.title: Strict and rigorous 2PL
children.definition: Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit, and rigorous 2PL holds all locks until commit, both easing recovery.

children.title: Deadlock and starvation
children.definition: Deadlock is a circular wait for locks and starvation is a transaction repeatedly losing the competition; both must be handled.

children.title: Lock conversion
children.definition: Upgrading a shared lock to exclusive or downgrading it the other way, which must respect the two phases.

topics.title: Timestamp Ordering and Validation Techniques
topics.definition: Timestamp ordering orders transactions by their start time, and validation methods check for conflicts only at commit time.

children.title: Timestamp ordering protocol
children.definition: Each item keeps the read and write timestamps of the last transaction that accessed it, and conflicting older operations are rejected and restarted.

children.title: Thomas write rule
children.definition: Ignores an obsolete write that a later transaction has already overwritten.

children.title: Optimistic (validation based) concurrency control
children.definition: Transactions run freely and are validated in three phases: read, validation and write.

children.title: Comparison with locking
children.definition: Timestamp and validation methods avoid deadlock because they never make a transaction wait for a lock.

topics.title: Granularity of Data Items
topics.definition: Granularity refers to the size of the unit locked, from a single field up to the whole database.

children.title: Trade-off of granularity
children.definition: Small items allow more concurrency but more lock overhead, while large items do the opposite.

children.title: Multiple granularity locking
children.definition: Locks are taken at several levels of the hierarchy with intention locks.

children.title: Intention shared and intention exclusive locks
children.definition: IS and IX locks on ancestors signal that a descendant will be locked in shared or exclusive mode.

children.title: Compatibility of intention locks
children.definition: The compatibility matrix decides which combinations may be granted at the same time.

topics.title: Recovery Concepts
topics.definition: Recovery restores the database to a consistent state after a failure and ensures committed work is not lost.

children.title: Types of failure
children.definition: Transaction failure, system crash, media failure and natural disasters need different recovery responses.

children.title: Storage structure and stable storage
children.definition: Volatile memory, non volatile disk and stable storage mirrored across sites define what survives a crash.

children.title: Log based recovery
children.definition: A log records before images, after images and transaction events; deferred and immediate update policies use it differently.

children.title: Checkpoints
children.definition: Periodically flush the log and buffers so that recovery need not scan the whole log.

children.title: Shadow paging
children.definition: Maintains a current and a shadow page table, switching atomically on commit, which avoids a log but fragments storage.

children.title: ARIES recovery algorithm
children.definition: Uses write ahead logging, repeating history and fuzzy checkpoints in analysis, redo and undo passes.

topics.title: Database Security Issues
topics.definition: Database security protects data from unauthorised access, disclosure and modification.

children.title: Access control and authorisation
children.definition: Discretionary and mandatory access control models grant privileges to users and roles.

children.title: Views and query modification
children.definition: Restricting a user to a view exposes only the rows and columns they may see.

children.title: Encryption and auditing
children.definition: Data is encrypted in storage or transit, and audit trails record who did what.

children.title: Statistical database security
children.definition: Statistical queries must not allow inference of individual values; techniques include query restriction, perturbation and auditing.

topics.title: File Organisation and Operations
topics.definition: A file is stored as records in blocks on disk, and its organisation decides how efficiently records are found and updated.

children.title: File operations
children.definition: Insertion, deletion, modification and retrieval of records identified by a search key.

children.title: Heap file organisation
children.definition: Records are placed wherever space is free, which makes insertion fast but search slow.

children.title: Sequential file organisation
children.definition: Records are kept in order of a search key, so search and ordered retrieval are fast while insertion needs reorganisation.

children.title: Hashing and indexed organisation
children.definition: A hash function or index computes the location directly, trading space and maintenance for speed.

children.title: Blocking factor and record layout
children.definition: Fixed or variable length records are packed into blocks, and the blocking factor is the records per block.

topics.title: Hashing Techniques
topics.definition: Hashing applies a function to the search key to compute the bucket where the record is stored.

children.title: Static hashing
children.definition: A fixed number of buckets is chosen in advance; the file grows slowly and long overflow chains appear.

children.title: Collision and overflow handling
children.definition: Open addressing, chaining within a bucket and multiple hashing resolve records that map to a full bucket.

children.title: Dynamic and extendible hashing
children.definition: The number of buckets grows and shrinks with the data by splitting buckets and using a directory of pointer bits.

children.title: Comparison of hashing with indexing
children.definition: Hashing is excellent for equality searches but useless for range queries, where indexes are preferred.

topics.title: Indexing and Types of Indexes
topics.definition: An index is an auxiliary file of key and pointer pairs that speeds up retrieval from the main file.

children.title: Primary index
children.definition: Built on the ordered key field of a sequentially ordered file, with one entry per block.

children.title: Clustering index
children.definition: Defined on an ordered non key field, so several records can share the same index value.

children.title: Secondary index
children.definition: Built on a non ordered field, giving one entry per distinct value with pointers to blocks.

children.title: Dense and sparse indexes
children.definition: A dense index has an entry for every search key value while a sparse index has entries for some values only.

children.title: Single level and multilevel indexes
children.definition: When the index itself becomes large it is indexed again, forming a multilevel structure like an ISAM tree.

children.title: Indexes on multiple keys
children.definition: Composite indexes order by the concatenation of keys, and grid or partitioned hashing handles multiattribute equality queries.

topics.title: B Tree and B+ Tree
topics.definition: B trees and B+ trees are balanced multilevel search structures designed for disk storage with a high branching factor.

children.title: B tree properties
children.definition: All leaves are at the same level, nodes hold between a minimum and maximum number of keys, and a node with k keys has k + 1 children.

children.title: B+ tree properties
children.definition: Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers while all data pointers live in a linked list of leaves.

children.title: Insertion in a B+ tree
children.definition: Insert into the correct leaf and split it when full, pushing the middle key into the parent and possibly splitting upwards to the root.

children.title: Deletion in a B+ tree
children.definition: Remove the entry, redistribute keys with a sibling or merge nodes when a node falls below the minimum occupancy.

children.title: B tree versus B+ tree
children.definition: B trees store data pointers in internal nodes and B+ trees do not, so B+ trees have higher fan-out and faster range scans.

children.title: Why B+ trees dominate databases
children.definition: A high fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so a record is found in three or four disk accesses even for millions of records.

topics.title: Object Oriented Database Management Systems
topics.definition: An OODBMS stores objects with their methods and supports the object oriented features of programming languages directly.

children.title: Need for OODBMS
children.definition: Applications with complex data such as CAD, multimedia and GIS suffer from the impedance mismatch between objects and tables.

children.title: Features
children.definition: Object identity, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and persistence are supported natively.

children.title: Object oriented data model
children.definition: Objects have identity and state, classes define types, and relationships are captured through references and collections.

children.title: Object oriented languages and persistence
children.definition: Languages such as C++ and Java are extended with a persistent object store, or pure OO languages such as Smalltalk are used.

children.title: Advantages and disadvantages
children.definition: Excellent for complex data and navigational access, but weak for ad hoc queries and lacking a common standard.

topics.title: Object Relational Databases
topics.definition: An object relational DBMS extends the relational model with objects, inheritance, complex types and methods.

children.title: Object relational features
children.definition: User defined types, collections such as arrays and nested tables, references and object identifiers.

children.title: Bridging objects and tables
children.definition: Object relational mapping persists programming objects as rows and columns.

children.title: Comparison of the three approaches
children.definition: RDBMS flatten complex data, OODBMS lose SQL simplicity and ORDBMS keep both, which is why commercial systems follow this route.

topics.title: XML and Semi-structured Data
topics.definition: XML is a text based, self describing format for exchanging hierarchical data between systems.

children.title: Structure of XML
children.definition: A prolog, nested elements with tags, attributes, entities and text content form a well formed document.

children.title: DTD and XML Schema
children.definition: Define the allowed elements, attributes and structure, so documents can be validated.

children.title: Parsing and querying XML
children.definition: DOM and SAX parsers read documents and XPath, XQuery and XSLT select and transform the data.

children.title: Storing XML in a database
children.definition: Documents may be stored as CLOB values, shredded into tables or kept in native XML columns.

topics.title: Temporal Databases
topics.definition: Temporal databases record time so that past, present and future states of the data can be queried.

children.title: Valid time and transaction time
children.definition: Valid time is when a fact is true in the real world; transaction time is when it was stored in the database.

children.title: Bitemporal databases
children.definition: Track both kinds of time, allowing corrections and audit of what the system believed at any moment.

children.title: Temporal operators
children.definition: Queries use operators such as overlaps, contains, precedes and during on time intervals.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Banking audit trails, medical records, insurance history and employee service records.

topics.title: Mobile Databases
topics.definition: A mobile database runs on portable devices and synchronises with a central database over wireless links.

children.title: Challenges
children.definition: Frequent disconnection, limited bandwidth, low battery and small memory change the design assumptions.

children.title: Data synchronisation and replication
children.definition: Changes made offline are reconciled later, which can raise conflicts that need resolution rules.

children.title: Mobile transactions
children.definition: Long lived, location dependent transactions require relaxed ACID properties in some systems.

topics.title: Spatial Databases
topics.definition: Spatial databases store geometric objects such as points, lines and polygons and answer location based queries.

children.title: Spatial data types and queries
children.definition: Point, line and region types support queries like "find all hospitals within 5 km".

children.title: Spatial indexing
children.definition: R trees, quad trees and grid files organise two dimensional data for fast region queries.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Geographic information systems, maps, navigation, urban planning and location based services.

topics.title: Case Study: Designing and Managing a Project Database
topics.definition: A case study ties the whole module together by taking one application from requirements to a working, normalised database.

children.title: Requirement analysis
children.definition: Identify entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and reports the users need.

children.title: Conceptual and logical design
children.definition: Draw the ER diagram, map it to relations, choose keys and normalise up to 3NF or BCNF.

children.title: Physical design and implementation
children.definition: Choose file organisation, indexes, constraints, views, triggers and the required privileges.

children.title: Maintenance and tuning
children.definition: Monitor performance, rebuild indexes, back up regularly and handle schema evolution.
